en.title: Economics: The Whole Degree Course
en.short: What economics is, how a BSc and MSc are organised, the main areas, and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Economics studies how people, firms and governments use scarce resources, and how their decisions combine into prices, output, incomes and growth. It is a social science with a strong mathematical and statistical side. Economists build simplified models, draw predictions from them, and test those predictions against data.

Two questions run through the subject. The first is positive: what happens if a price, a tax or an interest rate changes? The second is normative: what should a society do, given what happens? Evidence can settle much of the first question. The second also depends on values, such as how much weight to give to fairness against efficiency. This is one reason economists disagree. In this course, where schools of thought differ, each view is set out with its reasoning and evidence, and the choice is left to the reader.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
A BSc usually takes three years in the UK and South Africa, and four years in Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya. In Nigeria, programmes follow benchmarks set by the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics, under the National Board for Technical Education, award the ND and HND in related fields such as banking and finance, and colleges of education award the NCE. Details differ by institution, so always check your own handbook.

The first year introduces principles of economics, mathematics and statistics. The middle years deepen microeconomic and macroeconomic theory and add mathematical economics, econometrics, and applied fields. The final year usually includes a research project. A master’s degree repeats the core at a much higher technical level and ends with a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Foundations come first: scarcity, demand and supply, elasticity, consumer choice, production and costs, national income, and the simple Keynesian model, with the mathematics and statistics they need.

Microeconomic theory then covers market structures, game theory, factor markets, welfare and market failure. Macroeconomic theory covers IS-LM, aggregate demand and supply, inflation, unemployment and growth models. Mathematical economics adds matrix methods, constrained optimisation and dynamics. Econometrics teaches regression and its problems.

The applied fields follow: money and banking, public finance, international economics and development economics, together with the economic history and policy of Nigeria and Africa.

At master’s level, advanced microeconomics studies uncertainty, general equilibrium and information. Advanced macroeconomics studies dynamic models built on optimising households and firms. Advanced econometrics studies causal inference, panel data and time series. Research methods prepares you to write a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Economics is learned by doing problems. Read a section, close the book, and derive the result yourself. Then solve a new problem with different numbers. A model you can only describe is a model you do not yet understand.

Learn each model in three forms: words, a diagram and equations. Be able to move between them. When a variable changes, trace the effect step by step and state which curve shifts, in which direction, and why.

Connect theory to data early. Find national statistics from your own country and from another one, such as those of your statistics bureau, your central bank or the World Bank. Note the date and the definition of every number you use. Learn a statistical package, such as R, Stata or EViews, because employers and supervisors will expect it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students confuse a movement along a curve with a shift of the curve. They confuse a change in the price level with inflation, and nominal values with real ones. They treat an identity, such as S − I = X − M, as if it proved a cause.

In mathematics, many students forget to check the second-order condition, or solve a model without checking the answer in the original equations.

In econometrics, the most common error is to treat correlation as causation. Another is to report statistical significance without saying how large the effect is.

In policy essays, students often state one school’s view as if it were a fact. Name the assumption behind each conclusion, and say what evidence would change it. Finally, do not compare statistics across countries or years without checking that the method is the same. Rebased price indexes and new survey definitions can change a figure when the economy itself has not changed.

keyPoints: Economics studies choice under scarcity, in individual markets and in the whole economy.
Positive statements can be tested; normative statements also depend on values.
Learn every model in words, in a diagram and in equations.
Correlation does not prove causation.
Always check the date and definition of a statistic.

en.title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost and Economic Method
en.short: Scarcity, the production possibility frontier, positive and normative claims, and how models work.

sections.heading: Scarcity and opportunity cost
sections.text:
Resources such as labour, land, capital and entrepreneurial skill are limited, while wants are not. This is scarcity, and it forces choice. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative given up. For a student, the cost of a degree includes the wages she could have earned while studying.

Economists think at the margin. A rational decision-maker continues an activity until the marginal benefit, the gain from one more unit, equals the marginal cost, the cost of one more unit. Costs that are already paid and cannot be recovered are sunk costs. They should not affect the decision.

sections.heading: The production possibility frontier
sections.text:
The production possibility frontier (PPF) shows the largest combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology. Points on the frontier are productively efficient. Points inside it mean idle or badly used resources.

Worked example. With all its labour, a village can grow 100 tonnes of maize or make 50 units of cloth, and the frontier is a straight line.
Opportunity cost of 1 cloth = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 tonnes of maize.
Opportunity cost of 1 tonne of maize = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 cloth.

In practice the frontier usually bows outward. Resources are not equally suited to each good, so opportunity cost rises as more of one good is produced. Growth in resources or better technology shifts the frontier outward.

sections.heading: Method: models and claims
sections.text:
A model is a deliberate simplification. Its assumptions remove detail so that one relationship can be studied. Ceteris paribus means other things held constant. A good model is judged by what it explains and predicts, and also by how its assumptions affect its conclusions.

A positive statement describes what is, and can be tested: a higher minimum wage changes employment by some amount. A normative statement says what ought to be: the minimum wage should be raised.

keyPoints: Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up.
Decide at the margin and ignore sunk costs.
A bowed-out PPF shows rising opportunity cost.
Ceteris paribus means other things held constant.
Positive claims can be tested; normative claims also rest on values.

en.title: Demand, Supply and Market Equilibrium
en.short: Demand and supply functions, solving for equilibrium, shifts, and consumer and producer surplus.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text:
Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, other things constant. As price rises, quantity demanded normally falls. Income, tastes, expected prices and the prices of substitutes and complements all shift the demand curve.

Supply is the quantity sellers are willing to sell at each price. Higher prices normally call out more output, because marginal cost tends to rise. Input prices, technology, the number of sellers and taxes all shift the supply curve.

A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along a curve. A change in anything else causes a shift of the curve.

sections.heading: Solving for equilibrium
sections.text:
Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

Worked example. In a market for tomatoes, price P is in naira per kilogram and quantity Q is in tonnes.
Demand: Qd = 100 − 2P
Supply: Qs = −20 + 4P
Set Qd = Qs: 100 − 2P = −20 + 4P
120 = 6P, so P = 20
Q = 100 − 2(20) = 60
Check: Qs = −20 + 4(20) = 60. Both sides agree.

Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would pay and what they do pay. Demand reaches zero at P = 50, so:
Consumer surplus = ½ × 60 × (50 − 20) = 900
Producer surplus is the gap between the price received and the lowest price sellers would accept. Supply begins at P = 5, so:
Producer surplus = ½ × 60 × (20 − 5) = 450

sections.heading: Price controls
sections.text: A price ceiling set below equilibrium creates a shortage. In the example above, a ceiling of ₦15 gives Qd = 70 and Qs = 40, a shortage of 30. A price floor set above equilibrium creates a surplus. Supporters of such controls point to protection for poor buyers or small farmers. Critics point to the lost trade and suggest direct transfers instead.

keyPoints: A price change moves along a curve; other changes shift it.
Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Check any solution in both equations.
Surplus measures gains from trade.
A binding ceiling creates a shortage; a binding floor creates a surplus.

en.title: Elasticity of Demand and Supply
en.short: Price, income and cross elasticity, point and arc formulas, and the link with total revenue.

sections.heading: What elasticity measures
sections.text:
Elasticity measures how strongly one variable responds to another, in percentage terms.

Price elasticity of demand (PED) = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.

PED is usually negative. Demand is elastic if its absolute value is above 1, inelastic if below 1, and unit elastic at exactly 1. Close substitutes and a longer time make demand more elastic.

sections.heading: Point and arc formulas
sections.text:
For a small change, or a known demand function, use point elasticity:
PED = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)

Worked example. With Qd = 100 − 2P, at P = 20 and Q = 60:
PED = −2 × 20/60 = −0.67, which is inelastic.

For a larger change between two points, use arc elasticity, which takes the average of the start and end values as the base.

Worked example. A trader in Accra raises the price of a loaf from 45 to 55 cedis, and weekly sales fall from 110 to 90.
Change in Q = −20, average Q = 100, so −20%.
Change in P = +10, average P = 50, so +20%.
Arc PED = −20% ÷ 20% = −1, which is unit elastic.

sections.heading: Elasticity and revenue
sections.text:
If demand is inelastic, a price rise raises total revenue. If it is elastic, a price rise lowers total revenue. Revenue is greatest where demand is unit elastic.

Worked example. For Qd = 100 − 2P, TR = P(100 − 2P) = 100P − 2P².
dTR/dP = 100 − 4P = 0, so P = 25 and Q = 50.
PED there = −2 × 25/50 = −1, as expected.

sections.heading: Other elasticities
sections.text:
Income elasticity is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. It is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods.

Cross elasticity is the percentage change in the quantity of one good divided by the percentage change in the price of another. It is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.

keyPoints: PED = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q) at a point.
Use average values as the base for arc elasticity.
Total revenue is highest where demand is unit elastic.
Negative income elasticity marks an inferior good.
Positive cross elasticity marks substitutes; negative marks complements.

en.title: Consumer Choice: Utility and Indifference Curves
en.short: Utility, budget lines, indifference curves and how to find the best affordable bundle.

sections.heading: Preferences and utility
sections.text:
Consumer theory assumes that a person can rank bundles of goods. Preferences are assumed to be complete, so any two bundles can be compared, and transitive, so the ranking is consistent.

Utility is a number attached to each bundle to represent this ranking. Modern theory treats it as ordinal, meaning only the order matters. An older cardinal approach treated utility as measurable and stressed diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the one before.

An indifference curve joins bundles that give the same utility. Curves slope down, cannot cross, and are usually convex to the origin. The slope is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS), the amount of good y a person will give up for one more unit of good x. It equals MUx ÷ MUy, the ratio of marginal utilities.

sections.heading: The budget line
sections.text:
The budget line shows the bundles that cost exactly the consumer’s income:
Px·x + Py·y = m
Its slope is −Px/Py, the rate at which the market trades one good for the other. A rise in income shifts it outward in parallel. A change in one price rotates it.

sections.heading: Finding the best bundle
sections.text:
At an interior optimum, the highest reachable indifference curve just touches the budget line. Then MRS = Px/Py.

Worked example. Amina has utility U = xy and an income of ₦120. Px = 2 and Py = 3.
MUx = y and MUy = x, so MRS = y/x.
Tangency: y/x = 2/3, so y = 2x/3.
Budget: 2x + 3(2x/3) = 120, so 4x = 120.
x = 30 and y = 20. U = 600.
Check: 2(30) + 3(20) = 120. MRS = 20/30 = 2/3.

With this utility function she spends half her income on each good. Such constant shares are a feature of Cobb-Douglas preferences. Corner solutions are also possible: if the tangency condition cannot hold with both goods positive, she buys only one good.

keyPoints: An indifference curve joins bundles of equal utility.
MRS = MUx ÷ MUy.
At an interior optimum, MRS = Px/Py.
A change in income shifts the budget line; a change in one price rotates it.
Modern consumer theory needs only ordinal utility.

en.title: Production and Costs
en.short: Production functions, returns, cost curves, and choosing the cheapest mix of inputs.

sections.heading: Production
sections.text:
A production function shows the largest output obtainable from given inputs, such as Q = f(K, L), with capital K and labour L. In the short run at least one input is fixed. In the long run all inputs can vary.

The marginal product of labour is the extra output from one more worker. The law of diminishing returns says that, with capital fixed, marginal product eventually falls as labour rises.

Returns to scale describe what happens in the long run when all inputs rise in the same proportion. Output may rise by more than that proportion (increasing returns), by the same (constant returns), or by less (decreasing returns).

sections.heading: Short-run costs
sections.text:
Average cost (AC) is total cost per unit, and marginal cost (MC) is the cost of one more unit. MC passes through the lowest point of AC.

Worked example. TC = 50 + 2Q + 0.5Q², in thousands of shillings.
AC = 50/Q + 2 + 0.5Q and MC = dTC/dQ = 2 + Q.
Minimise AC: −50/Q² + 0.5 = 0, so Q² = 100 and Q = 10.
AC = 5 + 2 + 5 = 12. MC = 2 + 10 = 12.

sections.heading: Long-run cost minimisation
sections.text:
An isoquant joins input bundles giving the same output. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS), which equals MPL ÷ MPK. An isocost line joins bundles with the same cost, with slope −w/r, where w is the wage and r is the rental rate of capital. The cheapest bundle is where they touch: MPL/MPK = w/r.

Worked example. Q = √(KL), w = 4, r = 16, and the target output is Q = 100.
MPL/MPK = K/L, so K/L = 4/16 and L = 4K.
Q = √(K × 4K) = 2K = 100, so K = 50 and L = 200.
Cost = 4(200) + 16(50) = 1,600. Average cost = 16.

keyPoints: Diminishing returns is a short-run idea; returns to scale is a long-run idea.
MC passes through the lowest point of AC.
The cheapest input mix satisfies MPL/MPK = w/r.
Fixed costs do not affect marginal cost.
Constant returns to scale give a flat long-run average cost.

en.title: National Income Accounting
en.short: GDP by three methods, GNI, real and nominal values, deflators, rebasing and the limits of GDP.

sections.heading: Three ways to measure GDP
sections.text:
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period. Three approaches should give the same total, apart from measurement error.

The output approach adds value added: each firm’s sales minus its purchases from other firms. This avoids double counting.
Worked example. A farmer sells wheat for 100. A miller turns it into flour and sells it for 150. A baker sells the bread for 220.
Value added = 100 + 50 + 70 = 220, which equals the final sale.

The income approach adds wages, profits, rent and interest, with adjustments for indirect taxes, subsidies and depreciation.

The expenditure approach uses GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), which is consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports. Transfer payments such as pensions are excluded from G, because no output is bought.

sections.heading: Real, nominal and GNI
sections.text:
Worked example, in trillions of cedis, in an imaginary economy. C = 80, I = 25, G = 20, X = 30 and M = 15.
Nominal GDP = 80 + 25 + 20 + 30 − 15 = 140.
If GDP at base-year prices is 125, then the GDP deflator = 140 ÷ 125 × 100 = 112.
If net factor income from abroad is −5, then gross national income (GNI) = 140 − 5 = 135.

Nominal GDP uses current prices. Real GDP uses constant prices, so it tracks quantities.

sections.heading: Rebasing and limits
sections.text:
Rebasing updates the base year and the coverage of the accounts. In July 2025 Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics moved its base year from 2010 to 2019 and reported nominal GDP of ₦372.82 trillion for 2024. The reported size rose largely because of wider coverage and better measurement, so it should not be read as a sudden rise in output.

GDP leaves out most unpaid household work and much informal activity. It does not measure inequality, leisure or damage to the environment.

keyPoints: GDP counts final output, or the sum of value added.
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
Transfer payments are not part of G.
GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100.
GNI = GDP plus net factor income from abroad.
Rebasing can change measured GDP without a change in real activity.

en.title: The Simple Keynesian Model and the Multiplier
en.short: The consumption function, Keynesian cross, and government spending, tax and open-economy multipliers.

sections.heading: The model
sections.text:
John Maynard Keynes argued in 1936 that output in the short run is set by total spending, called aggregate expenditure. Prices are held fixed in this simple model.

The consumption function is C = a + bYd. Here a is autonomous consumption, Yd is disposable income, and b is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), the share of each extra unit of income that is spent. Equilibrium occurs where output equals planned spending: Y = C + I + G.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
C = 50 + 0.8(Y − T), I = 100, G = 50 and T = 50, in billions of rand.
Y = 50 + 0.8(Y − 50) + 100 + 50
Y = 50 + 0.8Y − 40 + 150
Y = 160 + 0.8Y
0.2Y = 160, so Y = 800.
Check: Yd = 750, C = 50 + 600 = 650, and 650 + 100 + 50 = 800.

The government spending multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − b) = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.
The tax multiplier = −b ÷ (1 − b) = −0.8 ÷ 0.2 = −4.
A tax cut has a smaller effect than a spending rise of the same size, because part of the cut is saved.
If G and T both rise by 10, Y rises by 50 − 40 = 10. This balanced budget multiplier equals 1.

sections.heading: Why the multiplier works, and its limits
sections.text:
Extra spending becomes someone’s income. Part of that income is spent again, and so on. The total is a geometric series: 1 + b + b² + … = 1 ÷ (1 − b).

In an open economy, part of each round goes on imports. With a marginal propensity to import m = 0.1, the multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8 + 0.1) = 3.33.

The model ignores interest rates and prices, which later models add. Estimates of multipliers vary widely, and economists disagree about their size.

keyPoints: Equilibrium is where output equals planned spending.
Spending multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) in the simplest model.
Tax multiplier = −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC).
Imports, taxes and saving are leakages that reduce the multiplier.
Real-world multiplier estimates vary widely.

en.title: Mathematics for Economists: Functions and Calculus
en.short: Functions, derivatives and rules, marginal analysis, optimisation and partial derivatives.

sections.heading: Functions and derivatives
sections.text:
Economic models use functions, such as cost as a function of output. Power, exponential and logarithmic functions are also common. A natural logarithm is useful because a small change in ln x is close to the percentage change in x.

The derivative dy/dx is the rate of change of y as x changes. In economics, “marginal” usually means a derivative: marginal cost is dTC/dQ.

Main rules:
Power rule: d(axⁿ)/dx = anxⁿ⁻¹
Product rule: d(uv)/dx = u′v + uv′
Quotient rule: d(u/v)/dx = (u′v − uv′) ÷ v²
Chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/du) × (du/dx)

sections.heading: Finding a maximum or a minimum
sections.text:
A first-order condition sets the derivative to zero. It finds a stationary point. A second-order condition then tells you which kind it is. A negative second derivative means a maximum, and a positive one means a minimum.

Worked example. A firm has demand P = 100 − 2Q and total cost TC = 20Q.
TR = PQ = 100Q − 2Q².
Profit π = 100Q − 2Q² − 20Q = 80Q − 2Q².
First-order condition: dπ/dQ = 80 − 4Q = 0, so Q = 20.
Second-order condition: d²π/dQ² = −4, which is negative, so this is a maximum.
P = 100 − 40 = 60 and π = 80(20) − 2(400) = 800.

sections.heading: Partial derivatives
sections.text:
Most economic variables depend on several others. A partial derivative changes one variable while holding the others fixed. For Q = √(KL):
∂Q/∂L = 0.5√(K/L)
This is the marginal product of labour. It falls as L rises, which shows diminishing returns.

This function is homogeneous of degree 1: multiplying K and L by t multiplies Q by t. So it has constant returns to scale.

Elasticities can be read from logarithms. In ln Q = a + b ln P, the coefficient b is the price elasticity, because d ln Q ÷ d ln P = b. This fact is widely used in regression work.

keyPoints: A marginal value is a derivative.
The first-order condition finds a stationary point; the second-order condition identifies it.
A partial derivative holds other variables fixed.
In a log-log equation, the slope is an elasticity.
Always check the second-order condition.

en.title: Statistics for Economists
en.short: Descriptive statistics, probability, sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and index numbers.

sections.heading: Describing data and probability
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is the average, and the median is the middle value. For skewed data such as incomes, the median is often more informative. Variance measures the spread around the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root.

By the central limit theorem, the mean of a large random sample is close to normally distributed, even if the population is not.

sections.heading: Testing a hypothesis
sections.text:
A hypothesis test asks whether sample evidence is consistent with a claim about a population. The null hypothesis H₀ is the claim being tested. A Type I error rejects a true H₀. A Type II error keeps a false H₀. The p-value is the probability, if H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one seen. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

Worked example. A survey of 25 traders in Kano gives a mean weekly profit of 52 (thousand naira), with a sample standard deviation of 10. Test H₀: μ = 48 at the 5% level, two-tailed.
Standard error = 10 ÷ √25 = 2.
t = (52 − 48) ÷ 2 = 2.00.
The critical value with 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064.
Since 2.00 < 2.064, we do not reject H₀.
95% confidence interval = 52 ± 2.064 × 2 = 47.87 to 56.13, which includes 48.

sections.heading: Index numbers
sections.text:
A Laspeyres index uses base-period quantities, and a Paasche index uses current quantities.

Worked example. Two goods have base prices of 2 and 4, and current prices of 3 and 5. Base quantities are 10 and 5, and current quantities are 8 and 6.
Laspeyres = (3×10 + 5×5) ÷ (2×10 + 4×5) × 100 = 55 ÷ 40 × 100 = 137.5.
Paasche = (3×8 + 5×6) ÷ (2×8 + 4×6) × 100 = 54 ÷ 40 × 100 = 135.

keyPoints: The median is often better than the mean for skewed data.
A p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true.
A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis.
Failing to reject H₀ does not prove it.
Laspeyres uses base quantities; Paasche uses current quantities.

en.title: Income and Substitution Effects
en.short: Splitting a price change into two effects, compensated demand, Giffen goods and duality.

sections.heading: Two effects of a price change
sections.text:
When the price of a good rises, two things happen. The good is now dearer relative to others, so the buyer substitutes away from it. This is the substitution effect, and it always works against the price change. The buyer is also poorer in real terms. This is the income effect. For a normal good it reduces demand further, and for an inferior good it raises demand.

If an inferior good’s income effect is larger than its substitution effect, quantity demanded rises with price. This is a Giffen good. It is rare, and evidence for it is limited.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Return to U = xy, m = 120, Px = 2 and Py = 3. The optimum was x = 30, y = 20 and U = 600. Now Px rises to 4.
New Marshallian demand: x = m ÷ (2Px) = 120 ÷ 8 = 15. Total effect = 15 − 30 = −15.

Hicksian decomposition: find the cheapest way to keep U = 600 at the new prices.
Tangency: y/x = 4/3, so y = 4x/3.
Utility: x(4x/3) = 600, so x² = 450 and x = 21.21. Then y = 28.28.
Substitution effect = 21.21 − 30 = −8.79.
Income effect = 15 − 21.21 = −6.21.
Check: −8.79 + (−6.21) = −15.

sections.heading: Duality
sections.text:
The Marshallian demand function x(P, m) comes from maximising utility subject to income. The Hicksian demand function h(P, U) comes from minimising spending subject to a utility level. The two problems are duals, meaning they lead to the same bundle when the numbers match.

The expenditure function e(P, U) gives the lowest spending needed to reach U. Its derivative with respect to a price is Hicksian demand. This result is Shephard’s lemma.

The Slutsky equation links the two kinds of demand:
∂x/∂Px = ∂h/∂Px − x(∂x/∂m)
The first term is the substitution effect. The second is the income effect.

keyPoints: Total effect = substitution effect + income effect.
The substitution effect always opposes the price change.
A Giffen good is an inferior good with a very strong income effect.
Hicksian demand holds utility fixed; Marshallian demand holds income fixed.
Shephard’s lemma: the price derivative of the expenditure function is Hicksian demand.

en.title: Perfect Competition and Monopoly
en.short: Profit maximisation, supply, shutdown, monopoly pricing, deadweight loss and price discrimination.

sections.heading: Perfect competition
sections.text:
In perfect competition, there are many small firms, an identical product, free entry and full information. Each firm is a price-taker, so its marginal revenue equals the market price P. Profit is greatest where P = MC.

Worked example. TC = 50 + 2Q + 0.5Q², so MC = 2 + Q. Let P = 20.
20 = 2 + Q, so Q = 18.
Profit = 20(18) − [50 + 36 + 162] = 360 − 248 = 112.
Profit attracts new firms, which lowers P. Long-run equilibrium is where P equals minimum AC. We found earlier that this is Q = 10 and P = 12, with zero economic profit.
A firm should shut down in the short run if P is below minimum average variable cost.

sections.heading: Monopoly
sections.text:
A monopolist is the only seller, protected by barriers to entry. It faces the market demand curve, so marginal revenue is below price.

Worked example. P = 100 − 2Q and MC = 20, a constant.
TR = 100Q − 2Q², so MR = 100 − 4Q.
MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 60.
Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800.
Under competition, P = MC = 20 and Q = 40.
Deadweight loss = ½ × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = 400.
Lerner index = (P − MC) ÷ P = 40 ÷ 60 = 0.67. It also equals 1 ÷ |elasticity|.

sections.heading: Price discrimination and regulation
sections.text:
Price discrimination charges different prices for the same good. In the third degree, groups such as students pay different prices, with lower prices for more elastic groups.

Natural monopoly occurs when one firm can serve the market at lower cost than several, as with electricity grids. Governments may regulate prices or own the firm. Views differ on regulation against public ownership.

keyPoints: All profit-maximising firms set MR = MC.
In perfect competition, MR = P.
A firm shuts down if P is below minimum AVC.
Monopoly restricts output and creates deadweight loss.
Lerner index = (P − MC) ÷ P = 1 ÷ |elasticity|.

en.title: Oligopoly and Monopolistic Competition
en.short: Cournot, Bertrand and Stackelberg models, collusion and monopolistic competition.

sections.heading: Monopolistic competition
sections.text: Monopolistic competition has many firms, free entry and differentiated products, such as restaurants or hair salons. Each firm sets MR = MC. Entry then removes economic profit. In long-run equilibrium, demand touches average cost on its downward slope. So each firm produces less than the output that minimises average cost. Economists disagree about whether this excess capacity is a real waste, because consumers also value variety.

sections.heading: Three oligopoly models
sections.text:
An oligopoly has a few firms whose decisions affect each other. In all the examples below, P = 100 − Q, where Q = q₁ + q₂, and MC = 10 for both firms, with no fixed cost.

Cournot: firms choose quantities at the same time.
Firm 1 profit = (100 − q₁ − q₂ − 10)q₁.
First-order condition: 90 − 2q₁ − q₂ = 0, so q₁ = (90 − q₂) ÷ 2. This is its reaction function.
By symmetry, q₁ = q₂ = q, so q = (90 − q) ÷ 2 and q = 30.
Q = 60, P = 40, and profit = 30 × 30 = 900 each.

Stackelberg: firm 1 moves first and knows firm 2’s reaction.
Firm 1 profit = (90 − q₁ − (90 − q₁)/2)q₁ = (45 − q₁/2)q₁.
First-order condition: 45 − q₁ = 0, so q₁ = 45 and q₂ = 22.5.
Q = 67.5 and P = 32.5. Profits are 1,012.5 and 506.25.

Bertrand: firms choose prices for an identical product. Each can win the whole market by slightly undercutting. So P falls to MC = 10, and Q = 90.

sections.heading: Collusion
sections.text: If the two firms act as one monopolist, then MR = 100 − 2Q = 10, so Q = 45 and P = 55. Total profit is 2,025, more than the Cournot total of 1,800. But each firm has a reason to cheat by producing more, so cartels are unstable.

keyPoints: Output ranks: monopoly < Cournot < Stackelberg < Bertrand in this example.
A reaction function gives a firm’s best output for each rival output.
Bertrand rivals with identical goods price at marginal cost.
Cartels are profitable but unstable, because each member gains by cheating.
Monopolistic competition has zero long-run profit and product variety.

en.title: Game Theory
en.short: Dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, backward induction and repeated games.

sections.heading: Basic ideas
sections.text:
Game theory studies decisions when each player’s result depends on what others do. A dominant strategy is best whatever others do. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which no player can gain by changing strategy alone.

In the prisoner’s dilemma, each player has a dominant strategy to defect, yet both would be better off if both cooperated.

sections.heading: Mixed strategies
sections.text:
Some games need randomised strategies. Each mixes so as to make the other indifferent.

Worked example. In a zero-sum game, Row’s payoffs are: T against L = 3, T against R = −1, B against L = −2, and B against R = 2. Column’s payoffs are the negatives.
Let Column play L with probability q. Row is indifferent if:
3q − (1 − q) = −2q + 2(1 − q)
4q − 1 = 2 − 4q, so q = 3/8.
Let Row play T with probability p. Column is indifferent if:
3p − 2(1 − p) = −p + 2(1 − p)
5p − 2 = 2 − 3p, so p = 1/2.
Value of the game to Row = 4(3/8) − 1 = 0.5.

sections.heading: Sequential and repeated games
sections.text:
In a sequential game, solve from the end using backward induction. The result is a subgame perfect equilibrium, which removes threats that are not credible.

Worked example. An entrant may stay out (payoffs: entrant 0, incumbent 10) or enter. After entry, the incumbent may fight (−2, 2) or accommodate (4, 5). The incumbent prefers 5 to 2, so it would accommodate. The entrant therefore enters. The threat to fight is not credible.

In an infinitely repeated game, cooperation can last if players value the future. Under a grim trigger strategy, one defection ends cooperation for ever. Cooperation holds if the discount factor δ meets:
δ ≥ (T − R) ÷ (T − P)
Here T is the temptation, R the reward and P the punishment payoff.

keyPoints: A Nash equilibrium has no profitable one-player deviation.
A Nash equilibrium need not be efficient.
In a mixed equilibrium, each player makes the other indifferent.
Backward induction removes threats that are not credible.
Repeated play can support cooperation if players are patient.

en.title: Factor Markets and Income Distribution
en.short: Marginal productivity, labour supply, monopsony, unions and competing theories of distribution.

sections.heading: Demand for and supply of labour
sections.text:
A firm hires labour until the marginal revenue product (MRP) equals the wage. MRP is marginal revenue times the marginal product of labour.

Labour supply comes from a choice between income and leisure. A higher wage has a substitution effect, because leisure costs more, so people work more. It also has an income effect, since people can afford more leisure. At high wages the income effect may dominate, so the supply curve can bend backward.

Human capital theory explains wage differences by education and skill.

sections.heading: Monopsony
sections.text:
A monopsony is a single buyer of labour, such as one large employer in a mining town. To hire more workers it must raise the wage for all, so the marginal cost of labour is above the wage.

Worked example. Labour supply is w = 10 + L, and MRP = 70 − 2L.
Total wage bill = (10 + L)L = 10L + L².
Marginal factor cost: MFC = 10 + 2L.
MRP = MFC: 70 − 2L = 10 + 2L, so L = 15.
Wage read from the supply curve: w = 10 + 15 = 25.
At L = 15, MRP = 40, so workers are paid less than their MRP.
In a competitive market, 70 − 2L = 10 + L, so L = 20 and w = 30.

sections.heading: Minimum wages and unions
sections.text:
In a competitive labour market, a minimum wage above equilibrium reduces employment. Under monopsony, it can raise both wages and employment, up to a limit. Empirical studies disagree on the size of the employment effect, and the answer depends on the level of the minimum and the country. Unions may raise wages and, on some views, reduce employment.

Marginal productivity is the neoclassical account of distribution. Classical, Marxian and post-Keynesian writers place more weight on bargaining power, class and institutions.

keyPoints: Firms hire labour until MRP equals the wage.
The labour supply curve can bend backward.
A monopsonist pays less than MRP and hires fewer workers.
A minimum wage can raise employment under monopsony.
Theories of distribution differ on the role of power and institutions.

en.title: Welfare Economics and Market Failure
en.short: Pareto efficiency, welfare theorems, externalities, public goods, information problems and policy responses.

sections.heading: Efficiency and the welfare theorems
sections.text:
An allocation is Pareto efficient if no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. It says nothing about fairness: a very unequal allocation can be efficient.

The first welfare theorem says that, under certain conditions, competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. The conditions include complete markets, no externalities and price-taking. The second says that any efficient allocation can be reached by competition after suitable lump-sum transfers.

sections.heading: Externalities
sections.text:
An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on a third party without payment.

Worked example. Demand is P = 100 − Q. The marginal private cost is MPC = 20 + Q. Each unit causes pollution costing 10.
Market result: 100 − Q = 20 + Q, so Q = 40 and P = 60.
Marginal social cost: MSC = 30 + Q.
Efficient result: 100 − Q = 30 + Q, so Q = 35 and P = 65.
A Pigouvian tax of 10 per unit brings the market to Q = 35.

Ronald Coase argued that, with clear property rights and low transaction costs, the parties could bargain to efficiency themselves. Critics note that when pollution affects many people, as with gas flaring in the Niger Delta, transaction costs are high.

sections.heading: Public goods, commons and information
sections.text:
A public good is non-rival and non-excludable, such as street lighting. Free riders can enjoy it without paying, so markets supply too little. A common resource, such as a fishery, is rival but hard to exclude. It tends to be overused. Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can sometimes manage commons well through local rules.

Information may be unequal between buyers and sellers. This creates adverse selection and moral hazard, which are studied at master’s level.

Market failure does not by itself prove that intervention will help. Public choice economists stress government failure: officials may have poor information or their own interests. Others argue that the state can correct markets and build capabilities.

keyPoints: Pareto efficiency says nothing about fairness.
A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost corrects the output level.
The Coase theorem needs low transaction costs.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable.
Government failure must be weighed against market failure.

en.title: The IS-LM Model
en.short: Deriving IS and LM curves, solving for income and interest, and fiscal and monetary policy.

sections.heading: The two curves
sections.text:
The IS-LM model, due to John Hicks (1937), interprets Keynes for a short run with fixed prices. It finds the income Y and the interest rate r that clear the goods and money markets together.

The IS curve shows pairs of Y and r with goods-market equilibrium. A higher r lowers investment and so lowers Y, so IS slopes down. The LM curve shows pairs with money-market equilibrium. Higher income raises money demand. So r must rise to restore balance, and LM slopes up.

sections.heading: Policy
sections.text:
Fiscal expansion: G rises by 20. IS becomes Y = 1,700 − 50r.
Solving gives r = 7 and Y = 1,350.
With r fixed, the multiplier of 5 would raise Y by 100. Here Y rises by only 50, because r rises by 1 and I falls by 10, which removes 50 of income. This is crowding out.

Monetary expansion: M/P rises by 25 to 525. LM becomes Y = 1,050 + 50r.
Solving gives r = 5.5 and Y = 1,325.

sections.heading: Limits and debates
sections.text: If money demand is highly sensitive to r, LM is flat. In this liquidity trap, monetary policy is weak and fiscal policy strong. Monetarists have argued that LM is steep and crowding out large. Keynesians have argued the reverse.

keyPoints: IS shows goods-market equilibrium; LM shows money-market equilibrium.
A rise in G shifts IS right and raises r.
A rise in M shifts LM right and lowers r.
Crowding out reduces the fiscal multiplier.
Curve slopes decide which policy is stronger.

en.title: Aggregate Demand, Aggregate Supply and Schools of Thought
en.short: AD and AS curves, supply shocks, stabilisation, and how the main macroeconomic schools differ.

sections.heading: The AD-AS framework
sections.text:
Aggregate demand (AD) shows the total quantity of output demanded at each price level. It slopes down mainly because a lower price level raises real money balances, which lowers interest rates and raises spending. Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) slopes up if wages or some prices are slow to adjust. Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) is vertical at potential output, which depends on resources and technology.

A demand shock moves output and prices in the same direction. A negative supply shock, such as a rise in oil prices, raises prices and lowers output at once. This mix is called stagflation.

sections.heading: Main schools
sections.text:
Classical view: prices and wages adjust, so output stays near potential. Money mainly affects prices.

Keynesian view: wages and prices can be slow to fall, and demand can stay too low for a long period. Fiscal and monetary policy can reduce recessions.

Monetarist view, associated with Milton Friedman: money growth is the main cause of changes in nominal income. Long and variable lags make fine-tuning risky, so a steady rule is preferred.

New classical view, associated with Robert Lucas: people form rational expectations, so systematic policy has little real effect. Real business cycle theory goes further and explains cycles by real shocks such as changes in productivity.

New Keynesian view: agents are rational, but prices and wages are sticky, for instance because of adjustment costs. So demand matters in the short run. This is a common basis of central bank models.

Post-Keynesian view: fundamental uncertainty, the role of finance and income distribution are central.

Structuralist views, influential in Latin America and Africa, stress bottlenecks in food, foreign exchange and infrastructure as causes of inflation and slow growth.

sections.heading: How to compare them
sections.text: Each school rests on assumptions about how quickly prices adjust, how expectations form, and how well governments can act. Evidence has moved these debates. The stagflation of the 1970s challenged early Keynesian models, while the 2008 financial crisis renewed interest in demand and finance.

keyPoints: A demand shock moves output and prices together.
A negative supply shock raises prices and lowers output.
Long-run aggregate supply is vertical in most models.
Schools differ on price flexibility, expectations and policy ability.
State each school’s assumptions before its conclusions.

en.title: Inflation and the Phillips Curve
en.short: Measuring inflation, its causes, the quantity theory, Fisher equation and Phillips curve.

sections.heading: Measuring inflation
sections.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. It is usually measured by the change in a consumer price index (CPI). Definitions matter. When Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics rebased its CPI, reported headline inflation moved from 34.80% in December 2024 (old method) to 24.48% in January 2025 (new method, with new weights and a 2024 base). Analysts treated much of this fall as a result of the method, so the two numbers cannot be compared directly.

sections.heading: Causes and theories
sections.text:
Demand-pull inflation comes from spending that exceeds productive capacity. Cost-push inflation comes from higher costs, such as fuel, wages or imports after a currency falls.

The quantity theory starts from an identity, MV = PY. With V (velocity) stable, it implies in growth rates: π ≈ money growth − output growth.
Worked example. Money grows by 20% and output by 3%. Exactly: 1.20 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 16.5%.
Monetarists read this as saying that money causes inflation in the long run. Others argue that velocity is unstable, or that money responds to prices.

The Fisher equation connects nominal interest i and real interest r: (1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + π).
Worked example. i = 20% and π = 15%. r = 1.20 ÷ 1.15 − 1 = 4.35%.

sections.heading: The Phillips curve
sections.text:
In 1958 A. W. Phillips found a negative link between UK wage growth and unemployment. Friedman and Edmund Phelps then argued that no lasting trade-off exists once people adjust their expectations. The modern form is:
π = πᵉ − β(u − uₙ) + v
Here πᵉ is expected inflation, uₙ is the natural rate of unemployment and v is a supply shock.

Worked example. πᵉ = 8, β = 0.5, uₙ = 6, u = 4 and v = 0.
π = 8 − 0.5(4 − 6) = 9.

In the long run, in this view, π = πᵉ, so the curve is vertical at uₙ.

keyPoints: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level.
CPI rebasing can change the reported rate.
MV = PY is an identity; the theory lies in assuming V is stable.
(1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + π) is the exact Fisher equation.
Expectations shift the Phillips curve.

en.title: Unemployment
en.short: Definitions, types, steady-state rate, wage theories, Okun’s law and Nigeria’s measurement debate.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text:
The International Labour Organization (ILO) counts as unemployed a person of working age who is without work, available for work and looking for work. The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed.

Worked example. Of 100 million people of working age, 57 million work and 3 million are unemployed.
Labour force = 60 million.
Unemployment rate = 3 ÷ 60 = 5%.

Definitions change results. Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics reported 33.3% for the fourth quarter of 2020 under its old method, which also counted many people working under 20 hours a week. Under a revised method aligned with ILO standards, it reported 4.1% for the first quarter of 2023, counting those who worked at least one hour in the previous week as employed. The bureau defended the change as an international standard. Critics said the new number hides weak job quality. Underemployment and informal work are essential parts of the picture in many African economies.

sections.heading: Types and the natural rate
sections.text:
Frictional unemployment comes from the time needed to find a job. Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch of skills or location, or from wages above market levels. Cyclical unemployment comes from a shortage of demand in a recession.

The natural rate is the rate at which the labour market is in steady state. If s is the rate of job loss and f is the rate of job finding, then:
u = s ÷ (s + f)
Worked example. With s = 0.02 and f = 0.18, u = 0.02 ÷ 0.20 = 10%.

sections.heading: Explanations and Okun’s law
sections.text:
Efficiency wage theory says that firms may pay above the market wage to raise effort and reduce turnover. Keynesians stress weak demand. Others stress regulation, the design of benefits or weak skills. The balance differs by country.

Okun’s law is an empirical link between output and unemployment. One version: output growth = 3 − 2 × (change in unemployment rate).

keyPoints: The unemployed are without work, available and seeking work.
The rate is unemployed ÷ labour force.
Nigeria’s 33.3% (Q4 2020) and 4.1% (Q1 2023) use different definitions.
Steady-state rate: u = s ÷ (s + f).
Okun’s law is an empirical pattern that varies by country.

en.title: Economic Growth Models
en.short: Harrod-Domar, Solow, golden rule, growth accounting and endogenous growth, with worked solutions.

sections.heading: Harrod-Domar
sections.text:
The Harrod-Domar model links growth to saving: g = s ÷ v, where s is the saving rate and v is the capital-output ratio.
Worked example. With s = 20% and v = 4, g = 5%.
The model assumes that capital and labour are not substitutes.

sections.heading: The Solow model
sections.text:
Robert Solow (1956) allowed substitution and diminishing returns to capital. In per-worker terms, y = f(k). Capital per worker changes by:
Δk = s·f(k) − (n + δ)k
Here n is population growth and δ is depreciation. In the steady state, investment just covers the capital that must be replaced.

Worked example. y = √k, s = 0.3 and n + δ = 0.1.
0.3√k = 0.1k, so √k = 3.
k = 9, y = 3 and c = (1 − 0.3) × 3 = 2.1.

A higher saving rate raises the level of income, but not its long-run growth rate. Long-run growth per head comes only from technical progress.

The golden rule is the steady state that maximises consumption. It requires MPK = n + δ. Here MPK = 0.5 ÷ √k, so √k = 5, k = 25 and y = 5.
Then s = 0.5 and c = 2.5, which is higher than 2.1.

sections.heading: Growth accounting
sections.text:
Output growth = TFP growth + α(capital growth) + (1 − α)(labour growth). TFP, total factor productivity, is the residual.
Worked example. Output grows by 5%, capital by 6% and labour by 2%, with α = 0.4.
TFP growth = 5 − 0.4(6) − 0.6(2) = 5 − 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.4%.

sections.heading: Endogenous growth and debate
sections.text:
Paul Romer and Robert Lucas modelled knowledge and human capital as outcomes of decisions. In the AK model, y = Ak, with no diminishing returns, so saving can raise growth permanently.

Solow predicts conditional convergence: poorer countries with similar fundamentals grow faster. Evidence supports this only partly. Others stress institutions (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson), geography, or structural change.

keyPoints: Harrod-Domar: g = s ÷ v.
Solow: Δk = s·f(k) − (n + δ)k.
Saving changes the level of income, but not long-run growth, in Solow.
Golden rule: MPK = n + δ.
TFP growth is the residual in growth accounting.
Endogenous growth treats technology as an outcome of decisions.

en.title: Matrix Algebra and Input-Output Analysis
en.short: Matrices, Cramer’s rule, solving linear models, and Leontief input-output analysis.

sections.heading: Why matrices
sections.text:
Economic models often form systems of linear equations. Matrices write them compactly as Ax = b, where A holds the coefficients, x the unknowns and b the constants. If the determinant of A is not zero, the system has a unique solution, x = A⁻¹b.

For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), the determinant is ad − bc. The inverse is (1 ÷ determinant) times the matrix with rows (d, −b) and (−c, a).

Cramer’s rule finds each unknown as a ratio of two determinants. To find a variable, replace its column in A with b, take the determinant, and divide by the determinant of A.

sections.heading: Leontief input-output analysis
sections.text:
Wassily Leontief described how industries buy from each other. Let aᵢⱼ be the input from sector i needed per unit of output of sector j. Output x must cover intermediate use and final demand d:
x = Ax + d, so x = (I − A)⁻¹d.

Worked example. a₁₁ = 0.2, a₁₂ = 0.3, a₂₁ = 0.4, a₂₂ = 0.1. Final demand is d₁ = 60 and d₂ = 30.
I − A has rows (0.8, −0.3) and (−0.4, 0.9).
Determinant = 0.72 − 0.12 = 0.6.
Inverse = (1 ÷ 0.6) × rows (0.9, 0.3) and (0.4, 0.8).
x₁ = (0.9 × 60 + 0.3 × 30) ÷ 0.6 = 63 ÷ 0.6 = 105.
x₂ = (0.4 × 60 + 0.8 × 30) ÷ 0.6 = 48 ÷ 0.6 = 80.
Check: 0.2(105) + 0.3(80) + 60 = 105, and 0.4(105) + 0.1(80) + 30 = 80.

The model assumes fixed coefficients and constant returns.

keyPoints: Ax = b has a unique solution if the determinant is not zero.
Cramer’s rule uses ratios of determinants.
Leontief: x = (I − A)⁻¹d.
Input-output analysis assumes fixed technical coefficients.
Always substitute the answer back to check it.

en.title: Constrained Optimisation and Comparative Statics
en.short: The Lagrangian method, the bordered Hessian, the meaning of the multiplier and comparative statics.

sections.heading: The Lagrangian method
sections.text:
To maximise f(x, y) subject to g(x, y) = c, form the Lagrangian:
L = f(x, y) + λ[c − g(x, y)]
Set the partial derivatives with respect to x, y and λ to zero and solve.

Worked example. Maximise U = xy subject to 2x + 3y = 120.
L = xy + λ(120 − 2x − 3y)
∂L/∂x = y − 2λ = 0
∂L/∂y = x − 3λ = 0
∂L/∂λ = 120 − 2x − 3y = 0
From the first two: y = 2λ and x = 3λ.
Substituting: 2(3λ) + 3(2λ) = 120, so 12λ = 120 and λ = 10.
So x = 30 and y = 20, with U = 600.

sections.heading: Second-order condition
sections.text:
The bordered Hessian checks whether the point is a maximum. Its first row and first column hold 0 and the constraint’s derivatives. The rest holds the second derivatives of L.
Here its rows are (0, 2, 3), (2, 0, 1) and (3, 1, 0).
Determinant = 0(0 − 1) − 2(0 − 3) + 3(2 − 0) = 6 + 6 = 12.
With two variables and one constraint, a positive determinant means a maximum.

sections.heading: The meaning of λ
sections.text:
The multiplier λ is the rate at which the optimal value rises as the constraint is relaxed. It is called a shadow price. Here it is the marginal utility of income: one more unit of income adds about 10 units of utility.
This is an example of the envelope theorem: the effect of a parameter on the optimal value is its direct effect in the Lagrangian.

When a constraint might not bind, or a variable may be zero, Kuhn-Tucker conditions are used.

sections.heading: Comparative statics
sections.text: Comparative statics asks how the solution moves when a parameter changes. When a model cannot be solved directly, take total differentials of the first-order conditions, then solve the linear system for the changes. Cramer’s rule is often used.

keyPoints: Form L = f + λ(c − g), then set the partial derivatives to zero.
Check the bordered Hessian for the type of optimum.
λ is a shadow price.
Kuhn-Tucker conditions handle inequality constraints.
Comparative statics traces how a solution moves with a parameter.

en.title: Economic Dynamics: Difference and Differential Equations
en.short: Stability, the cobweb model, and continuous growth over time.

sections.heading: Why dynamics
sections.text: Static models show where an economy ends up. Dynamic models show the path over time and whether it reaches a resting point at all. Time may be treated as separate periods, which leads to difference equations, or as continuous, which leads to differential equations.

sections.heading: First-order difference equations
sections.text:
Consider xₜ = a·xₜ₋₁ + b, with a ≠ 1. The steady state, where x stays fixed, is x̄ = b ÷ (1 − a). The general solution is:
xₜ = x̄ + (x₀ − x̄)aᵗ
The path converges to x̄ if |a| < 1. If a is negative, it swings from side to side as it moves.

Worked example, the cobweb model. A farmer decides output using last season’s price.
Demand: Qdₜ = 100 − 2Pₜ
Supply: Qsₜ = −20 + Pₜ₋₁
Market clearing: 100 − 2Pₜ = −20 + Pₜ₋₁
Pₜ = 60 − 0.5Pₜ₋₁
Steady state: P̄ = 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40. Check: Qd = 20 and Qs = 20.
From P₀ = 44: P₁ = 38, P₂ = 41, P₃ = 39.5.
The gaps from 40 are +4, −2, +1, −0.5. So |a| = 0.5 gives a stable, oscillating path.
If |a| were above 1, the swings would grow. The path is stable if supply is less sensitive to price than demand is.
The model assumes that farmers expect the last price to continue. Rational expectations would remove the swings.

sections.heading: Differential equations
sections.text:
Let x(t) change continuously, with dx/dt = gx. The solution is x(t) = x₀eᵍᵗ, which is exponential growth at rate g.

Worked example. An amount of 100 grows at a continuous rate of 10% for 2 years: 100 × e raised to the power 0.2 = 122.14.
At a continuous 5% growth rate, doubling takes ln 2 ÷ 0.05 = 13.86 years. This explains the rule of 70 used in growth work.

keyPoints: Steady state of xₜ = axₜ₋₁ + b is b ÷ (1 − a).
The path is stable if |a| < 1.
A negative a gives oscillation.
dx/dt = gx gives x(t) = x₀eᵍᵗ.
Doubling time = ln 2 ÷ g.

en.title: Regression Analysis: Ordinary Least Squares
en.short: The linear model, OLS estimates step by step, R², t tests, and the Gauss-Markov assumptions.

sections.heading: The model
sections.text:
Regression estimates how a dependent variable Y changes with an explanatory variable X:
Yᵢ = α + βXᵢ + uᵢ
Here uᵢ is an error term, which holds all other influences. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses the estimates a and b that minimise the sum of squared residuals. A residual is the gap between the actual Y and its fitted value.

b = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ Σ(X − X̄)²
a = Ȳ − bX̄

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Income X and consumption Y for five households, in thousands of rand per month:
X: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Y: 12, 19, 29, 37, 43
X̄ = 30 and Ȳ = 28.
Σ(X − X̄)² = 400 + 100 + 0 + 100 + 400 = 1,000.
Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) = 320 + 90 + 0 + 90 + 300 = 800.
b = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 0.8. a = 28 − 0.8(30) = 4.
Fitted values: 12, 20, 28, 36, 44. Residuals: 0, −1, 1, 1, −1.
RSS = 4. Total sum of squares = 644. R² = 1 − 4 ÷ 644 = 0.994.
Error variance = 4 ÷ (5 − 2) = 1.33.
Standard error of b = √(1.33 ÷ 1,000) = 0.0365.

Test H₀: β = 0. t = 0.8 ÷ 0.0365 = 21.9. The 5% two-tailed critical value with 3 degrees of freedom is 3.182. So we reject H₀.
Interpretation: each extra thousand rand of income goes with 0.8 thousand more consumption. Five observations are too few for real work.

sections.heading: Assumptions and extensions
sections.text:
Under the Gauss-Markov assumptions, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE). These are: a model linear in parameters, no perfect collinearity, a zero mean for errors given X, constant error variance, and no correlation between errors.

Multiple regression includes several variables. Each coefficient measures the effect of one, with the others held constant.

keyPoints: OLS minimises the sum of squared residuals.
b = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ Σ(X − X̄)².
A t test divides (b − hypothesised value) by the standard error.
A high R² does not prove causation.
Under Gauss-Markov assumptions, OLS is BLUE.

en.title: When Regression Assumptions Fail
en.short: Multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, omitted variables, endogeneity and their remedies.

sections.heading: Multicollinearity
sections.text: Multicollinearity means that explanatory variables are highly correlated. Estimates remain unbiased, but standard errors become large. The variance inflation factor measures this: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ comes from regressing one X on the others. If R²ⱼ = 0.9, VIF = 10, so the variance of that coefficient is ten times larger than it would be with no correlation. Dropping a relevant variable to fix it can cause bias.

sections.heading: Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation
sections.text:
Heteroskedasticity means the error variance is not constant. OLS stays unbiased, but the usual standard errors are wrong. Tests include Breusch-Pagan and White. Remedies are robust standard errors, or weighted least squares if the form of the variance is known.

Autocorrelation means errors are correlated over time, which is common in time series. OLS is again unbiased if the regressors are exogenous, but standard errors are wrong. The Durbin-Watson statistic is about 2(1 − ρ), where ρ is the correlation between successive errors. So ρ = 0.5 gives a value near 1, and a value near 2 suggests no first-order autocorrelation. Remedies include Newey-West standard errors, or a better dynamic specification.

sections.heading: Omitted variables and endogeneity
sections.text:
Endogeneity means that an explanatory variable is correlated with the error. Then OLS is biased, and more data will not fix it. This is the most serious of these problems.

Omitted variable bias is one source. In a regression of wages on schooling, ability may be left out. If the true effect of schooling is β, the effect of ability on wages is γ, and δ is the slope from regressing ability on schooling, then the expected estimate is β + γδ.
Worked example. β = 0.08, γ = 0.05 and δ = 0.4. The expected estimate = 0.08 + 0.05 × 0.4 = 0.10, which overstates the effect.

Other sources are simultaneity, such as price and quantity determined together, and measurement error in X. Instrumental variables, experiments and panel methods are the main remedies.

keyPoints: Multicollinearity inflates standard errors but does not bias OLS.
Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation mainly make standard errors wrong.
Durbin-Watson ≈ 2(1 − ρ).
Endogeneity biases OLS and does not disappear with more data.
Omitted variable bias = γδ.

en.title: Money and Commercial Banking
en.short: Functions of money, money demand, how banks create deposits, the money multiplier and bank risk.

sections.heading: Money and its demand
sections.text:
Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. Narrow money (M1) is currency plus demand deposits. Broad money adds savings and time deposits.

Keynes named three motives for holding money: transactions, precaution and speculation. Interest is the cost of holding money, so money demand falls as interest rises.

sections.heading: How banks create money
sections.text:
Banks accept deposits and make loans. On a bank’s balance sheet, assets are reserves, loans and securities. Liabilities are deposits and borrowing. Capital is assets minus liabilities. When a bank lends, it credits the borrower’s account, which creates a new deposit.

The textbook money multiplier links broad money M to the monetary base B (currency plus reserves):
m = (1 + c) ÷ (c + r)
where c is the currency-to-deposit ratio and r is the reserve ratio.
Worked example. c = 0.2, r = 0.1 and B = 500 (billion cedis).
m = 1.2 ÷ 0.3 = 4, so M = 4 × 500 = 2,000.

Many central banks now target an interest rate instead of reserves. On this view, bank lending depends on demand and on capital, and reserves then follow. Treat the multiplier as an accounting relation, not a fixed rule.

sections.heading: Bank risk and regulation
sections.text:
Banks borrow short and lend long, so they face liquidity risk and possible runs. Regulators respond with deposit insurance, liquidity rules and capital rules.

In Nigeria, the Central Bank’s 2004 directive raised minimum capital from ₦2 billion to ₦25 billion by the end of 2005. The number of banks fell from 89 in 2004 to 25. In March 2024 it set new minimums of ₦500 billion (international), ₦200 billion (national) and ₦50 billion (regional licences) for commercial banks, with a deadline of 31 March 2026. Supporters expect stronger banks that can finance large projects. Critics fear greater concentration and less attention to small firms. Rules change, so check the regulator’s current circulars.

keyPoints: Money has three functions.
Multiplier: m = (1 + c) ÷ (c + r).
Loans create deposits, but lending is limited by demand, capital and policy.
Bank capital absorbs losses.

en.title: Central Banking and Monetary Policy
en.short: Policy tools, transmission channels, inflation targeting, the Taylor rule, independence and African practice.

sections.heading: Tools
sections.text:
A central bank issues currency, acts as banker to government and to banks, and supervises parts of the financial system. Its main tools are the policy rate, open market operations (buying and selling securities), reserve requirements and lending to banks.

In Nigeria, the Central Bank of Nigeria began operations in 1959, and its Monetary Policy Committee sets the Monetary Policy Rate.

sections.heading: How policy reaches the economy
sections.text:
Transmission runs through several channels. Interest rates change borrowing and investment. Asset prices change wealth and spending. The exchange rate changes net exports and import prices. Credit availability changes lending to firms. Expectations can shift prices and wages directly. These effects take time, and the lags can be long.

In many African economies, these channels are weaker, because few households borrow from banks, the government may be the main borrower, and food and fuel supply shocks are large.

sections.heading: Rules, targets and independence
sections.text:
Under inflation targeting, the central bank publicly commits to an inflation goal and adjusts policy to reach it. South Africa has targeted inflation since 2000, and Ghana since 2007. The UK has a target of 2%. Other frameworks target the exchange rate or a monetary aggregate.

A Taylor rule describes how a central bank might set its rate:
i = rₙ + π + 0.5(π − πᵗ) + 0.5(output gap)
where rₙ is the neutral real rate and πᵗ is the target.
Worked example. rₙ = 2, π = 4, πᵗ = 2 and the output gap = 1.
i = 2 + 4 + 0.5(2) + 0.5(1) = 7.5.
A coefficient on inflation above 1 overall means that the real rate rises when inflation rises.

The time-inconsistency argument of Kydland and Prescott (1977) says that a policymaker may promise low inflation, then be tempted to inflate later. Independent central banks are one answer. Critics raise questions of democratic accountability, and they argue that central banks should also weigh jobs or development.

keyPoints: The policy rate is the main tool of most central banks.
Transmission works through interest rates, assets, exchange rates, credit and expectations.
Taylor rule: i = rₙ + π + 0.5(π − πᵗ) + 0.5(gap).
Time inconsistency is the classic case for independence.
Transmission can be weaker where few households use banks.

en.title: Public Finance and Taxation
en.short: Why governments spend, principles of tax, tax incidence and deadweight loss, worked step by step.

sections.heading: Roles of government
sections.text:
Richard Musgrave described three functions of government: allocating resources where markets fail, redistributing income, and stabilising the economy. How much of each a state should do is a matter of debate, not just of analysis.

For a public good, the efficient amount is where the sum of all people’s marginal benefits equals the marginal cost. This is the Samuelson rule.

sections.heading: Principles of taxation
sections.text:
Adam Smith’s canons of taxation are equity, certainty, convenience and economy. A tax is progressive if the share of income paid rises with income, regressive if it falls, and proportional if it is constant. Direct taxes fall on income or wealth. Indirect taxes fall on spending.

The Ramsey rule says that, for efficiency alone, goods with inelastic demand should have higher tax rates. Equity may point the other way, as such goods are often necessities.

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 took effect on 1 January 2026, and it consolidated several federal tax laws. Value added tax (VAT) stayed at 7.5%. Rates and thresholds change, so check the current official sources.

sections.heading: Tax incidence: a worked example
sections.text:
Incidence is who really bears a tax. It does not depend on who legally pays, but on elasticities. The less elastic side bears more.

Demand: Qd = 100 − 2P. Supply before tax: Qs = −20 + 4P, so P = 20 and Q = 60.
A tax of ₦6 per unit is placed on sellers. They keep P − 6:
Qs = −20 + 4(P − 6) = −44 + 4P
100 − 2P = −44 + 4P, so P = 24 and Q = 52.
Buyers pay 24, which is 4 more. Sellers keep 18, which is 2 less.
Tax revenue = 6 × 52 = 312.
Deadweight loss = ½ × 6 × (60 − 52) = 24.

The deadweight loss grows roughly with the square of the tax rate.

keyPoints: The Samuelson rule: the sum of marginal benefits equals marginal cost.
Who legally pays a tax does not decide who bears it.
The less elastic side bears more of a tax.
Deadweight loss rises roughly with the square of the tax.
Nigeria’s VAT remained at 7.5% under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025; check current rules.

en.title: Government Budgets, Public Debt and Fiscal Federalism
en.short: Deficits, debt dynamics, Ricardian equivalence, Laffer curve, debt distress and revenue sharing.

sections.heading: Budgets and debt dynamics
sections.text:
The primary balance excludes interest payments. Sustainability depends on the debt ratio, not on the amount alone.

The debt ratio d changes as follows:
Δd = [(r − g) ÷ (1 + g)]d − p
where r is the real interest rate on debt, g is real growth and p is the primary surplus as a share of GDP.

Worked example. Debt is 60% of GDP, with r = 8% and g = 5%. The primary surplus that holds the ratio constant is:
p = (0.03 ÷ 1.05) × 60 = 1.71% of GDP.

sections.heading: Debates
sections.text:
Ricardian equivalence, revived by Robert Barro in 1974, says that households know that debt today means taxes later. So they save a tax cut, and borrowing has no effect on demand. Critics point to borrowing limits, short horizons and imperfect foresight.

Keynesians hold that deficits support demand in a recession and that early cuts may reduce growth. Those concerned about debt stress crowding out, risk premiums and the loss of market access. Empirical work has not settled the size of these effects, and estimates of a dangerous debt threshold are disputed.

The Laffer curve shows that revenue is zero at tax rates of 0% and 100%, so that it peaks somewhere in between. Where the peak lies is an empirical question, and it varies by country and tax.

sections.heading: Debt distress in Africa
sections.text: Zambia defaulted on a Eurobond payment in November 2020. Ghana halted payments on most external debt in December 2022. Both then sought relief under the G20 Common Framework, agreed in November 2020. Observers have discussed slow progress and the difficulty of coordinating official and private creditors.

sections.heading: Fiscal federalism
sections.text: Federal systems divide taxes and spending between levels of government. In Nigeria, the Federation Account Allocation Committee shares federally collected revenue among the federal, state and local governments. This raises debates on dependence on oil revenue, on how much states should raise themselves, and on the shares of oil-producing areas.

keyPoints: The primary balance excludes interest.
Debt-stabilising primary surplus = (r − g)d ÷ (1 + g).
Ricardian equivalence relies on strong assumptions.
The peak of the Laffer curve is an empirical question.
Zambia and Ghana both sought relief under the G20 Common Framework.

en.title: International Trade Theory and Policy
en.short: Comparative advantage, Heckscher-Ohlin, new trade theory, tariffs and the debate over protection.

sections.heading: Why countries trade
sections.text:
David Ricardo showed that trade can benefit both sides even if one country is more productive at everything.

Worked example. Output per worker per day:
Country A: 6 cocoa or 3 cloth, so 1 cloth costs 2 cocoa.
Country B: 2 cocoa or 2 cloth, so 1 cloth costs 1 cocoa.
A has an absolute advantage in both. But cocoa is relatively cheaper in A (1 cocoa costs 0.5 cloth) than in B (1 cocoa costs 1 cloth). So A has a comparative advantage in cocoa, and B in cloth. Both gain at terms of trade between 1 and 2 cocoa per cloth.

The Heckscher-Ohlin model says a country exports goods that use its abundant factor intensively. Stolper-Samuelson adds that trade raises the real return of the abundant factor and lowers that of the scarce one, so it creates winners and losers. New trade theory (Krugman) explains trade between similar countries by economies of scale.

sections.heading: Tariffs: a worked example
sections.text:
A small country has demand Qd = 120 − P and supply Qs = P. The world price is 20.
Free trade: Qd = 100, Qs = 20 and imports = 80.
Tariff of 10: price = 30, Qd = 90, Qs = 30 and imports = 60.
Consumer surplus loss = ½(100 + 90) × 10 = 950.
Producer surplus gain = ½(20 + 30) × 10 = 250.
Government revenue = 10 × 60 = 600.
Net loss = 950 − 250 − 600 = 100.

sections.heading: The debate on protection
sections.text:
The standard view is that free trade raises total welfare, while transfers can help those who lose. Infant industry arguments hold that new industries need time behind protection to learn. Supporters cite Korea and Taiwan. Critics cite failed attempts elsewhere, and protection that is hard to remove.

Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued that the terms of trade of primary exporters tend to fall over time. Later evidence is mixed.

keyPoints: Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost, not absolute productivity.
Heckscher-Ohlin: export goods that use your abundant factor.
Trade creates winners and losers within a country.
A tariff’s net loss is two deadweight triangles for a small country.
Infant-industry protection remains debated.

en.title: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
en.short: BOP accounts, saving and investment identity, PPP, interest parity, Marshall-Lerner and the policy trilemma.

sections.heading: The accounts
sections.text:
The balance of payments records a country’s transactions with the rest of the world. The current account covers trade in goods and services, net income from abroad and transfers, including remittances. The capital and financial accounts cover assets, loans and reserves. Together, with errors and omissions, they sum to zero.

An identity links the current account to saving: CA = S − I, with S as national saving and I as investment. If saving is 20% of GDP and investment 25%, the current account deficit is 5% of GDP. An identity shows no cause.

sections.heading: Exchange rate theories
sections.text:
Purchasing power parity (PPP) says that a currency’s value should move to offset price differences. In relative form, the rate of depreciation is about equal to the inflation difference.
Worked example. Inflation is 20% at home and 3% abroad. Expected depreciation = 1.20 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 16.5%.
PPP holds better over long periods and is weak in the short run.

Uncovered interest parity says that the gap in interest rates equals expected depreciation.
Worked example. Interest is 18% at home and 5% abroad. 1.18 ÷ 1.05 − 1 = 12.4% expected depreciation.

A devaluation improves the trade balance only if export and import elasticities sum to more than 1 in absolute value. This is the Marshall-Lerner condition.

sections.heading: Policy choices
sections.text:
The Mundell-Fleming model extends IS-LM. With high capital mobility, monetary policy is strong under floating rates, while fiscal policy is strong under fixed rates. This leads to the impossible trinity: a country cannot have a fixed rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy all at once.

Nigeria moved to a more market-based rate in June 2023 and allowed the naira to fall sharply. Supporters said this removed distortions and arbitrage. Critics stressed the sharp rise in living costs. Views also differ on whether devaluation helps economies where exports do not respond much to price, such as oil exporters.

keyPoints: CA = S − I is an identity, not a theory.
Relative PPP links depreciation to inflation differences.
UIP links the interest gap to expected depreciation.
Marshall-Lerner: the elasticities must sum to more than 1.
The impossible trinity: a fixed rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy cannot all hold.

en.title: Measuring Development, Poverty and Inequality
en.short: GDP per head, HDI, poverty lines and FGT measures, the Gini coefficient and multidimensional poverty.

sections.heading: What development means
sections.text: Development means more than higher income. Amartya Sen defines it as an expansion of capabilities: what people are able to be and do. The Human Development Index (HDI), used by the United Nations Development Programme since 1990, combines health, education and income. It takes the geometric mean of the three indices, so a very low score in one cannot be fully offset by a high score in another.

sections.heading: Measuring poverty
sections.text:
The poverty line is the income needed for a minimum standard of living. Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) measures build on it.
The headcount ratio is the share below the line.
The poverty gap measures how far below the line people are, on average, counting the non-poor as zero.

Worked example. Five people have incomes of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10, and the line is 5.
Headcount = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.
Poverty gap = [(4 + 3 + 2 + 1) ÷ 5] ÷ 5 = 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4.

Multidimensional measures count shortages in areas such as health, education and living standards. Nigeria’s 2022 Multidimensional Poverty Index survey, released in November 2022, found about 133 million people, or 63% of the population, to be multidimensionally poor. The same report compared this with monetary poverty of 40% in 2018/19.

sections.heading: Measuring inequality
sections.text:
The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of people, starting from the poorest. The Gini coefficient measures the gap from the line of equality. It runs from 0 (full equality) to 1.

Worked example. For the same five people, total income = 20. Cumulative shares are 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.50 and 1.
G = 1 − 0.2 × [(0 + 0.05) + (0.05 + 0.15) + (0.15 + 0.30) + (0.30 + 0.50) + (0.50 + 1)]
G = 1 − 0.2 × 3 = 0.4.

Different Lorenz curves can give the same Gini, so the single figure hides information.

keyPoints: Sen defines development as an expansion of capabilities.
HDI combines health, education and income.
Headcount ignores how far below the line people are; the poverty gap does not.
Gini runs from 0 to 1.
Nigeria’s 2022 survey counted about 133 million people as multidimensionally poor.

en.title: Theories of Economic Development
en.short: Linear stages, structural change, dependency, market reform, institutions and evidence-based approaches.

sections.heading: Stages and structural change
sections.text:
W. W. Rostow (1960) described five stages of growth, with a take-off that requires higher saving and investment. Critics note that the order is not universal and that the stages explain little about causes.

W. Arthur Lewis (1954) described a dual economy. A traditional sector has surplus labour with low marginal product. A modern sector can hire from it at a nearly constant wage, so profits and investment grow. Critics ask how much surplus labour really exists, and note that modern firms may use little labour.

Rosenstein-Rodan’s big push argues that industries depend on each other’s demand, so coordinated investment is needed.

sections.heading: Dependency and structuralism
sections.text: Dependency theorists, such as Andre Gunder Frank and Samir Amin, argued that the world system locks poor countries into a subordinate role. Critics point to the rapid growth of export-oriented economies in East Asia, and to the costs of protected and inefficient industries.

sections.heading: Market reform and its critics
sections.text: From the 1980s, neoclassical economists blamed price distortions and state failure for slow growth. The policy package later called the Washington Consensus included fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation and market-based exchange rates. Supporters argue that it restored stability. Critics, among them Joseph Stiglitz and Thandika Mkandawire, argue that it cut social spending and neglected industrial capacity.

sections.heading: Current approaches
sections.text:
Institutional economists argue that property rights and the limits on power shape long-run growth. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson linked modern institutions to colonial history, and they shared the 2024 Nobel memorial prize. Their data and interpretation have also been challenged.

New structural economics, associated with Justin Yifu Lin, favours a state that supports industries in line with comparative advantage. Ha-Joon Chang argues that rich countries themselves used protection in the past.

Randomised controlled trials, used by Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer, test specific policies, such as school inputs or subsidies for health products. Critics question whether such results can be generalised and whether small tests can answer big questions.

keyPoints: Lewis: surplus labour moves from traditional to modern sectors.
Dependency theory stresses unequal relations in the world system.
The Washington Consensus favoured market-based reforms.
Institutions, capabilities and trials are major current approaches.
State each theory’s evidence as well as its claim.
