en.title: Nigerian Economic History up to 1986
en.short: Colonial economy, marketing boards, development plans, oil boom, Dutch disease and the 1980s crisis.

sections.heading: Colonial foundations
sections.text: Before colonial rule, the areas that became Nigeria had long-distance trade, crafts and farming. Colonial policy from the late nineteenth century turned exports towards cash crops such as palm produce, cocoa and groundnuts, moved by railways built to the ports. Marketing boards, formed from the 1940s, bought export crops at fixed prices. They were presented as a way to stabilise farm incomes. Critics, including Peter Bauer, argued that they taxed farmers heavily.

sections.heading: Independence and planning
sections.text:
The Central Bank of Nigeria began operating in 1959, and independence came in 1960. Four national development plans ran between 1962 and 1985. They emphasised public investment and import-substituting industry. The civil war of 1967 to 1970 caused great loss of life and damage.

Crude oil was found at Oloibiri in 1956, and exports grew through the 1960s. Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971. The naira replaced the pound in 1973, on a decimal basis. Indigenisation decrees in 1972 and 1977 reserved some activities and shares for Nigerians. Supporters stress national control. Critics say that a narrow group benefited.

sections.heading: Oil boom and Dutch disease
sections.text:
The oil price rises of the 1970s brought large revenues. The state expanded capital projects and public pay, including the Udoji award of 1974. Meanwhile agricultural exports declined and food imports grew.

The Dutch disease model (Corden and Neary, 1982) explains how this can occur. A resource boom raises the real exchange rate and pulls labour and capital into the booming and non-tradable sectors. Other tradable sectors, such as farming and manufacturing, then shrink. Writers also point to other causes of farm decline, including drought, the war, price policy and urban bias. How much weight each deserves is disputed.

sections.heading: The early 1980s crisis
sections.text: When oil prices fell in the early 1980s, revenue and foreign exchange fell. The government responded in 1982 with an Economic Stabilization Act, cutting imports through controls. A national debate in late 1985 considered an IMF loan, which the public largely opposed. The government then adopted its own Structural Adjustment Programme in 1986.

keyPoints: Colonial policy tied exports to cash crops.
Marketing boards were meant to stabilise farm incomes; critics argued that they taxed farmers heavily.
Oil was found at Oloibiri in 1956; Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971.
Dutch disease shrinks other tradable sectors after a resource boom.
The oil price fall of the early 1980s led towards SAP in 1986.

en.title: Nigeria’s Economy and Policy Since 1986
en.short: SAP and its debate, reforms of the 2000s, recessions, subsidy and exchange rate reform from 2023.

sections.heading: SAP and its debate
sections.text:
The Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) began in 1986. It devalued the naira through a Second-tier Foreign Exchange Market, ended commodity boards, liberalised trade and interest rates, and began privatisation.

Supporters note a recovery in non-oil exports and farm output in the following years, and argue that earlier controls could not continue. Critics point to falling real wages, weaker public services, deindustrialisation and social unrest. Assessment is hard. Oil prices fell at the same time, policy reversals were frequent, and it is unclear what would have happened otherwise.

sections.heading: The 2000s
sections.text: After the return to civilian rule in 1999, reform included the National Economic Empowerment and Development Strategy (NEEDS) of 2004 and the 2004 to 2005 bank consolidation. In October 2005 the Paris Club agreed a deal under which Nigeria would pay about US$12.4 billion and receive cancellation of about US$18 billion. Economists debate how much of the strong growth that followed came from reform and how much from oil prices.

sections.heading: Oil dependence and shocks
sections.text: Oil remains central to foreign earnings. In the third quarter of 2023, crude oil was about 82.5% of total merchandise exports, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Yet the rebased GDP accounts of 2025 show services at about 53% of GDP in 2019, the base year. Lower oil prices contributed to recession in 2016, and the pandemic with an oil price fall contributed to another in 2020.

sections.heading: Reforms from 2023
sections.text: In May 2023 the new government announced the end of the petrol subsidy. In June 2023 it moved to a more market-based exchange rate, and the naira fell sharply. Inflation rose strongly. The IMF and World Bank backed the changes on fiscal and efficiency grounds, arguing that subsidies were costly and benefited richer households more. Critics, including labour groups, pointed to severe effects on living costs and argued that support for poor households came too slowly. Whether the longer-term gains outweigh the short-term costs is a question that later data will inform.

keyPoints: SAP began in 1986 and remains debated.
SAP’s effects are hard to separate from oil price changes.
The Paris Club deal of 2005 cancelled about US$18 billion.
Oil is a large share of exports but a smaller share of GDP.
Subsidy and exchange rate reforms began in 2023, and their long-term effects are debated.

en.title: African Economic Policy and Integration
en.short: Post-independence strategies, Lagos Plan and Berg Report, adjustment, currency unions and AfCFTA.

sections.heading: After independence
sections.text:
Many African states pursued state-led industrial strategies after independence, often with support from marketing board or commodity revenues. Oil shocks, falling commodity prices and rising debt then produced severe problems in many countries from the late 1970s.

Two documents framed the debate. The Lagos Plan of Action (1980), from the Organisation of African Unity, stressed self-reliance and blamed much of the crisis on external shocks and unequal trade. The World Bank’s Berg Report (1981) stressed domestic policy errors, such as overvalued exchange rates and heavy taxes on farmers.

sections.heading: Adjustment and growth
sections.text:
Structural adjustment programmes spread during the 1980s and 1990s. Ghana’s Economic Recovery Programme of 1983 was widely described by supporters as a success, with renewed growth. Critics point to weak industrial change and new dependence on aid and gold and cocoa exports.

Growth improved in many African economies from around 2000, helped by reforms, by commodity demand and by fewer conflicts, with the mix varying by country.

sections.heading: The resource curse and diversity
sections.text: Economists have asked why resource wealth often goes with slow growth. Explanations include Dutch disease, price volatility, weak institutions and conflict. Botswana is often cited as a counter-example, where diamonds went with long periods of growth under stable institutions.

sections.heading: Integration and currencies
sections.text:
Regional bodies include ECOWAS (founded 1975) and the East African Community. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement entered into force on 30 May 2019, and trading under it officially began on 1 January 2021. Supporters expect wider markets, more manufacturing and more trade within Africa. Sceptics stress poor transport, slow implementation of rules of origin, and uneven gains.

The CFA franc zones link West and Central African currencies to the euro, with roots in the colonial period. Supporters cite low inflation and stability. Critics cite lost policy freedom and limited competitiveness. Optimum currency area theory, from Robert Mundell, asks whether members share similar shocks and have mobile labour. This is central to debates on a single ECOWAS currency.

keyPoints: Lagos Plan stressed external causes; Berg Report stressed domestic policy.
Adjustment outcomes remain debated across African countries.
The resource curse is not inevitable: Botswana is often cited.
AfCFTA entered into force on 30 May 2019, with trading from 1 January 2021.
Optimum currency area theory asks if countries share shocks and have mobile labour.

en.title: Advanced Microeconomics: Uncertainty and General Equilibrium
en.short: Expected utility, risk aversion, exchange economies, Walras’ law and existence of equilibrium.

sections.heading: Choice under uncertainty
sections.text:
Von Neumann and Morgenstern showed that if preferences over lotteries satisfy certain axioms, including independence, they can be represented by expected utility: EU = Σ pᵢu(xᵢ). A concave u means risk aversion.

Worked example. A trader has a 50% chance of 400 and a 50% chance of 0, and u(x) = √x.
Expected value = 200.
EU = 0.5 × 20 + 0.5 × 0 = 10.
Certainty equivalent: √x = 10, so x = 100.
Risk premium = 200 − 100 = 100.

The Arrow-Pratt coefficient of absolute risk aversion is −u″ ÷ u′. The Allais paradox shows choices that break the independence axiom. Kahneman and Tversky’s prospect theory explains such choices with loss aversion and distorted probabilities. Behavioural economists treat these as central. Others consider expected utility a useful approximation in many markets.

sections.heading: General equilibrium in exchange
sections.text:
In an exchange economy, consumers hold endowments and trade at market prices. Walras’ law says the value of excess demand sums to zero across all markets. So if all markets but one clear, the last clears too, and only relative prices matter.

Worked example. Consumers A and B each have U = √(xy). A holds (8, 2) and B holds (2, 8). Let Py = 1 and Px = p.
Each spends half of their wealth on x.
xA = (8p + 2) ÷ (2p) and xB = (2p + 8) ÷ (2p).
Market clearing: (10p + 10) ÷ (2p) = 10, so 10p + 10 = 20p and p = 1.
xA = 5, and by the budget, yA = 5. In the same way, B gets (5, 5).
Check: both have MRS = y/x = 1 = p.

sections.heading: Existence and uniqueness
sections.text:
Arrow and Debreu (1954) proved that equilibrium exists under conditions including convex preferences and technology.

Sonnenschein, Mantel and Debreu showed that aggregate excess demand can take almost any shape, so uniqueness and stability do not follow from individual rationality.

keyPoints: Concave utility means risk aversion.
Risk premium = expected value − certainty equivalent.
Walras’ law: if all markets but one clear, the last clears too.
Arrow-Debreu proved that equilibrium exists; uniqueness needs more.
Prospect theory challenges expected utility with evidence on behaviour.

en.title: Information, Contracts and Mechanism Design
en.short: Adverse selection, signalling, moral hazard, principal-agent models, auctions and mechanism design.

sections.heading: Adverse selection
sections.text:
Adverse selection occurs when one side knows the quality of a good and the other does not. George Akerlof’s 1970 market for lemons shows how trade can collapse.

Worked example. Used cars have quality θ, uniformly distributed from 0 to 100. A seller values a car at θ and a buyer at 1.5θ. Buyers cannot see θ. At price p, only cars with θ ≤ p are offered.
Average quality of offered cars = p ÷ 2.
A buyer’s expected value = 1.5 × p ÷ 2 = 0.75p.
Since 0.75p < p at any positive p, no buyer will pay p. Trade fails, although every sale would be efficient under full information.

Michael Spence (1973) showed that informed agents can signal quality through costly actions. Education can signal ability if it costs able workers less, even if it adds no skill. Rothschild and Stiglitz (1976) showed that uninformed parties can screen by offering a menu, such as insurance contracts with different deductibles.

sections.heading: Moral hazard
sections.text:
Moral hazard arises when actions are hidden after a contract is signed. In a principal-agent problem, the principal wants high effort, but the agent bears its cost. Paying a fixed wage removes risk from the agent but gives no incentive. Paying a share gives incentive but puts risk on the agent. So an optimal contract trades off risk and incentive.

Group lending in microfinance uses peer monitoring to reduce moral hazard, although later trials have found modest average effects on income.

sections.heading: Mechanism design
sections.text:
Mechanism design asks how to design rules so that self-interested players produce a desired outcome. The revelation principle says that any outcome of a mechanism can also be achieved by one in which truthfully reporting one’s private information is optimal.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy, since your bid does not set your price. These ideas are used in spectrum sales and treasury bill auctions.

keyPoints: Adverse selection comes from hidden information.
Moral hazard comes from hidden actions.
A signal must cost low types more than high types.
Optimal contracts trade off risk and incentives.
Truthful bidding is dominant in a second-price auction.

en.title: Advanced Macroeconomics: Dynamic Models
en.short: Consumption Euler equation, Ramsey model, real business cycles, New Keynesian models, Lucas critique.

sections.heading: Intertemporal choice
sections.text:
With utility Σβᵗu(cₜ), the Euler equation is:
u′(cₜ) = β(1 + r)u′(cₜ₊₁)
It says that the gain from consuming one unit less today, saved at r, must match the loss today.

Worked example. Two periods with log utility, y₁ = 100, y₂ = 110, r = 0.1 and β = 1/1.1.
Euler: c₂/c₁ = β(1 + r) = 1, so c₁ = c₂ = c.
Lifetime budget: c + c/1.1 = 100 + 110/1.1 = 200.
c × (2.1/1.1) = 200, so c = 104.76.
Saving in period 1 = 100 − 104.76 = −4.76, which is borrowing.

sections.heading: Growth with optimal saving
sections.text: The Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans model makes saving a choice, unlike the Solow model. Its steady state satisfies f′(k) = δ + ρ + θg, where ρ is the rate of time preference, θ is the curvature of utility and g is technical progress.

sections.heading: Business cycle models
sections.text:
The Lucas critique (1976) argued that estimated relations change when policy changes, because expectations change. So policy models should rest on preferences and technology.

Real business cycle (RBC) models, such as Kydland and Prescott (1982), explain cycles as optimal responses to technology shocks, with flexible prices. Critics doubt that technology shocks are large enough, and they question the labour supply responses required.

New Keynesian dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models add sticky prices. A basic version has three equations:
IS: xₜ = Eₜxₜ₊₁ − (1/σ)(iₜ − Eₜπₜ₊₁ − rₙ)
Phillips curve: πₜ = βEₜπₜ₊₁ + κxₜ
Policy rule: iₜ = rₙ + φπ·πₜ + φx·xₜ
Here x is the output gap. A central result, the Taylor principle, is that φπ above 1 helps to ensure a stable solution.

sections.heading: Current debates
sections.text: After 2008, DSGE models were criticised for neglecting finance and differences among households. Newer work adds banks, heterogeneous agents and the zero lower bound. Post-Keynesian and agent-based critics argue that the method itself is flawed. Defenders reply that it makes assumptions explicit.

keyPoints: Euler equation: u′(cₜ) = β(1 + r)u′(cₜ₊₁).
Ramsey makes saving an optimal choice.
The Lucas critique says estimated relations can shift with policy.
RBC models stress real shocks; New Keynesian models add sticky prices.
Taylor principle: raise the policy rate by more than any rise in inflation.

en.title: Advanced Econometrics: Causal Inference and Panel Data
en.short: Maximum likelihood, limited dependent variables, IV and 2SLS, panels, difference-in-differences and RDD.

sections.heading: Estimation beyond OLS
sections.text: Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters that make the observed data most probable. When Y is binary, such as employed or not, probit and logit models keep predicted probabilities between 0 and 1. Their coefficients are not marginal effects, so compute and report the marginal effects.

sections.heading: Instrumental variables
sections.text:
An instrument Z must be relevant (correlated with X) and valid, meaning it affects Y only through X. Two-stage least squares (2SLS) first regresses X on Z, then regresses Y on the fitted X.

Worked example, the Wald estimator. Z is a binary rule. Mean Y is 30 where Z = 1 and 25 where Z = 0. Mean X is 12 where Z = 1 and 10 where Z = 0.
Estimate = (30 − 25) ÷ (12 − 10) = 2.5.

Validity cannot be fully tested when there is just one instrument per regressor, so it must be argued. A first-stage F statistic that is small signals a weak instrument, which leads to bias and unreliable inference. Imbens and Angrist (1994) showed that, with varying effects, IV estimates a local average effect for those whose X responds to Z.

sections.heading: Panel data
sections.text: Panels follow units over time. Fixed effects estimation removes all time-invariant differences between units. It cannot estimate effects of variables that do not change. Random effects assumes those traits are uncorrelated with the regressors. The Hausman (1978) test compares the two estimators.

sections.heading: Designs for causal effects
sections.text:
Difference-in-differences compares the change in a treated group with the change in a control group.
Worked example. Treated: 10 before and 16 after. Control: 12 before and 15 after.
Estimate = (16 − 10) − (15 − 12) = 3.
It relies on parallel trends, the assumption that both groups would have moved alike without treatment.

Regression discontinuity compares units just above and below a cutoff, such as an admission score. It estimates a local effect at that cutoff.

keyPoints: Report marginal effects for probit and logit.
An instrument must be relevant and valid.
IV identifies a local average treatment effect.
Fixed effects remove time-invariant differences.
Difference-in-differences relies on parallel trends.

en.title: Time-Series Econometrics
en.short: Stationarity, ARMA models, unit roots, cointegration, error correction, VARs and volatility models.

sections.heading: Stationarity and ARMA models
sections.text:
A series is weakly stationary if its mean, variance and autocovariances do not change over time. Standard inference relies on this.

Worked example, an AR(1) process. yₜ = 2 + 0.5yₜ₋₁ + eₜ, where e has variance σ².
Mean = 2 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 4.
Variance = σ² ÷ (1 − 0.25) = 1.33σ².

ARMA models combine autoregressive and moving-average parts.

sections.heading: Unit roots and spurious regression
sections.text:
A random walk, yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + eₜ, has a unit root. Shocks last permanently, and variance grows with time. Regressing one unrelated random walk on another often gives a high R² and large t values. This is spurious regression, shown by Granger and Newbold (1974).

The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test estimates Δyₜ = α + γyₜ₋₁ + lags, with H₀: γ = 0 (a unit root). It uses special critical values. KPSS reverses the null hypothesis.

sections.heading: Cointegration and error correction
sections.text:
Non-stationary series are cointegrated if some linear combination of them is stationary. They then share a long-run relationship. Engle and Granger (1987) proposed a two-step test, and Johansen’s method handles several relations. ARDL bounds testing is popular in applied work with small samples and mixed orders of integration.

An error correction model shows short-run changes and the adjustment back to the long run:
Δyₜ = a + bΔxₜ − 0.25(yₜ₋₁ − cxₜ₋₁) + eₜ
Here 25% of any gap closes each period.
Half-life = ln 0.5 ÷ ln 0.75 = 2.41 periods.

sections.heading: VARs and volatility
sections.text:
Christopher Sims (1980) proposed vector autoregressions (VARs), in which each variable depends on lags of all variables. Impulse responses trace the effect of a shock. Identification needs further assumptions, such as an ordering of variables or sign restrictions, and results can depend on them. Granger causality tests whether past X helps to predict Y. It is not causation in the ordinary sense.

ARCH (Engle) and GARCH (Bollerslev) models let the variance of errors depend on past shocks.

keyPoints: Standard inference needs stationarity or cointegration.
Regressions of unrelated random walks can look significant.
ADF has a unit root as its null hypothesis.
An error correction model shows the speed of adjustment to the long run.
Granger causality is about prediction, not causation.

en.title: Research Methods and the Dissertation
en.short: Framing a question, identification, data, sample size, writing up and research ethics in economics.

sections.heading: From topic to question
sections.text:
A good research question is specific, answerable with available data, and of real interest. “Effects of bank reform in Nigeria” is a topic. “Did the 2004 to 2005 bank consolidation change lending to small firms?” is a question.

A literature review is not a list of summaries. Organise it around debates, methods and gaps, and show what your study adds. Use primary sources where possible, including working papers from NBER, the World Bank and the African Economic Research Consortium.

sections.heading: Design and data
sections.text:
State your identification strategy: what variation allows you to say that X causes Y, and what could undermine this claim. If the design only shows a correlation, say so.

Data sources include national statistics bureaus, central bank bulletins, the World Bank’s World Development Indicators and Living Standards Measurement Study, the IMF’s data, and Afrobarometer. Check for changes in definitions and base years, as with Nigeria’s changes to CPI, GDP and unemployment measurement.

For a survey, estimate the sample size needed. To estimate a mean within ±E at 95% confidence:
n = (1.96σ ÷ E)²
Worked example. With σ = 20 and E = 4: n = (1.96 × 20 ÷ 4)² = 96.04, so survey at least 97. Add more for non-response and clustering. For tests of effects, run a power calculation, because a small study may miss a real effect.

sections.heading: Honest analysis and ethics
sections.text:
Running many specifications and reporting only the significant ones is called p-hacking. Pre-analysis plans and robustness checks reduce this risk. Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, not stars alone. Keep your code and data organised so that another person can reproduce your results.

Research involving people usually needs approval from an ethics committee. Obtain informed consent, protect privacy, and avoid harm.

sections.heading: The structure of a dissertation
sections.text: A typical structure is: introduction, literature review, theory or conceptual framework, data and method, results, discussion, and conclusion.

keyPoints: A question is narrower than a topic.
State your identification strategy and its threats.
Check data definitions and base years.
Report effect sizes as well as significance.
Ethical approval and consent are usually required for research with people.
